items.question: What ritual preparation qualifies a person to perform recitation and worship effectively?
premises: Breath placement is a prescribed method
One may perform this method first
Recitation and worship follow this method
items.inference: A person who first performs the breath-placement method is qualified to perform recitation and worship.
items.plain_english: Whoever performs the method of breath placement and then does recitation and worship.

items.question: What exalted status is attained by one who performs recitation and worship after breath placement?
premises: The qualified practitioner is identified emphatically
He is called divine and heroic
He is identified as Bhairava himself
items.inference: Such a practitioner is truly divine, a hero, and Bhairava himself.
items.plain_english: He indeed is a divine hero, and he indeed is Bhairava himself.

rows.grounds: ca + anyathā; in no other way

items.question: How should the qualified practitioner be regarded by others, according to the goddess?
premises: The practitioner is compared to the sun
He is worthy of worship
He is a true guru and no other way is valid
items.inference: Such a practitioner must be regarded as worshipful and a true guru, without exception.
items.plain_english: O goddess, he is the sun, worthy of worship, and a true guru, and not otherwise.

items.question: What disqualifying condition undermines the performance of recitation as a sacred sacrifice?
premises: This tantra can be unknown to a person
A person may still perform recitation sacrifice
Performance without knowledge is contrasted
items.inference: Performing recitation sacrifice without knowing this tantra is a deficient condition.
items.plain_english: But whoever performs the sacrifice of recitation without knowing this tantra.

items.question: What is the spiritual condition of one who acts as guru without knowing this tantra?
premises: Such a person may act as guru among all
Even as a disciple he remains bound
His condition is compared to an animal always
items.inference: One who teaches without knowing this tantra remains perpetually in a bound, animal-like state.
items.plain_english: O goddess, even if he is a guru to all, he is always like an animal, even as a disciple.

items.question: What benefit do recitation and worship bring to one who remains spiritually bound?
premises: The ignorant practitioner becomes bound
He may still perform recitation and worship
The value of these acts is questioned
items.inference: Recitation and worship are of no real benefit to one who remains bound in ignorance.
uncertainties: siktaḥ may also suggest being sprinkled or affected; taken here as bound/fettered in context
items.plain_english: O fair-limbed one, he becomes bound; what use are recitation and worship for him?

items.question: What improper change in mantra practice is prohibited regarding counting methods?
premises: A previous mantra may be abandoned
Another counting method may be adopted
This change is presented as a rule to consider
items.inference: One should not abandon a previous mantra and take up another merely for counting.
items.plain_english: Having abandoned the previous mantra, one should not take up another for the sake of counting.

items.question: What negative consequence may arise from focusing on counting the mantra?
premises: Mantra counting is singled out as a cause
A person may incur sin from it
The consequence is stated as a possibility
items.inference: A person may incur sin from counting the mantra.
items.plain_english: O goddess, whatever sin a person may obtain from counting the mantra.

items.question: How severe is the sin of mantra counting compared to disturbing a self-born liṅga?
premises: Sin may arise from mantra counting
Sin may arise from moving a self-born liṅga
The two are equated in gravity
items.inference: The sin from mantra counting is compared to the sin of moving a self-born liṅga.
items.plain_english: O goddess, it is like the sin one may obtain by moving a self-born liṅga.

items.question: What practical instruction follows from the grave fault attributed to mantra counting?
premises: Mantra counting is said to incur grave sin
A wise person is addressed
Avoidance is prescribed as the response
items.inference: A wise person should therefore avoid counting the mantra.
items.plain_english: Therefore, O goddess, a wise person should avoid counting.

items.question: Does the prohibition against counting extend beyond this mantra to all vidyās?
premises: Counting is prohibited in the prior context
All vidyās are included in scope
Avoidance is again prescribed
items.inference: A person should avoid counting in all other vidyās as well.
items.plain_english: In all other vidyās as well, a person should avoid counting.

items.question: What supreme attainment results from knowing the teaching that replaces mere counting?
premises: There is a knowledge to be attained
The practitioner who knows it acts accordingly
The result is reaching the rare abode of Brahman
items.inference: By knowing this, the practitioner attains the hard-to-reach abode of Brahman.
items.plain_english: Having known which, the practitioner goes to the hard-to-attain abode of Brahman.

items.question: Through which subtle channel and method should the breath be expelled in this practice?
premises: Expulsion of breath is prescribed
The piṅgalā path is specified
The action follows the sequence of breath control
items.inference: One should expel the breath through the piṅgalā path in the sequence of breath control.
items.plain_english: O beloved, one should expel the breath along the path of piṅgalā in the sequence of breath control.

items.question: What specific form of the mātṛkā letters is to be used in this breath practice?
premises: The mātṛkā consists of fifty letters
The letters are accompanied by bindu
They are joined with nāda
items.inference: The practice uses the fifty mātṛkā letters together with bindu and nāda.
items.plain_english: The fifty mātṛkā letters, accompanied by bindu and joined with nāda.

items.question: In what sequence should the mātṛkā letters be recited after the initial expulsion?
premises: The recitation follows a prior step
The mātṛkā letters are the object
The sequence specified is reverse order
items.inference: After that, one should recite the mātṛkā letters in reverse order.
items.plain_english: Then, O beloved, one should recite the mātṛkā letters in reverse order.

items.question: How should the mātṛkā be contemplated during recitation in forward and reverse order?
premises: Recitation occurs in natural and reverse order
The mātṛkā is the object of contemplation
She is to be visualized as youthful
items.inference: One should visualize the mātṛkā as youthful while reciting in forward and reverse order.
items.plain_english: One should visualize the youthful mātṛkā in natural order and in reverse order.

items.question: By what method should the breath expulsion through piṅgalā be performed?
premises: A specific method has been described
Breath expulsion is to be done again
The piṅgalā path is the locus of expulsion
items.inference: One should expel the breath through the piṅgalā path by this very method.
items.plain_english: By this very method, one should expel the breath along the path of piṅgalā.

items.question: At what times of day should this prescribed practice be performed?
premises: The practice is to be performed by someone
Three daily junctures are specified
The instruction is given as a prescription
items.inference: One should perform this practice at the three daily junctures.
items.plain_english: O trembling-eyed one, O lotus-faced one, whoever should do this at the three junctures.

items.question: How is the frequency of this practice adjusted for the Kali age?
premises: The practice may be done once
The context of the Kali age is specified
The number becomes fourfold in that age
items.inference: In the Kali age, performing it once is equivalent to a fourfold measure.
items.plain_english: Or once, O great goddess; in the Kali age the number is fourfold.

items.question: Where is the letter a placed in the bodily mapping of mātṛkā elements?
premises: The letter a is introduced as a topic
A bodily locus is assigned to it
The listener is asked to attend
items.inference: The letter a is assigned to the mouth as its elemental locus.
items.plain_english: Listen, O fair-complexioned one: the letter a is the element of the mouth.

items.question: Which bodily locations are assigned to the letters u and ū in the mātṛkā mapping?
premises: The letter u is given a location
The letter ū is given a location
Right and left ears are specified respectively
items.inference: The letter u is placed in the right ear and the letter ū in the left ear.
items.plain_english: The letter u should be in the right ear, and the letter ū in the left ear.

items.question: Which bodily locations are assigned to the letters ḷ and ḹ in the mātṛkā mapping?
premises: The letter ḷ is given a location
The letter ḹ is given a location
Right and left cheeks are specified respectively
items.inference: The letter ḷ is placed on the right cheek and the letter ḹ on the left cheek.
items.plain_english: The letter ḷ should be on the right cheek, and the letter ḹ on the left cheek.

items.question: Which bodily locations are assigned to the letters o and au in the mātṛkā mapping?
premises: The letter o is given a location
The letter au is given a location
Upper and lower teeth are specified respectively
items.inference: The letter o is placed at the upper teeth and the letter au at the lower teeth.
items.plain_english: The letter o should be at the upper teeth, and the letter au at the lower teeth.

items.question: Where are the five elements beginning with the letter ka located in the body?
premises: A group of five elements beginning with ka is identified
A bodily location is assigned to them
This placement is commended
items.inference: The five elements beginning with ka are placed in the right arm.
items.plain_english: The five elements beginning with ka are commended as being in the right arm.
